title: Matthew (21 September)
hookLine: a tax collector at his table hears two words and gets up

cards: A table by the road, coins stacked on it, a ledger open. The man behind it collects taxes, and in the gospels his trade is named in the same breath as sinners. Nobody stops to chat.
Then someone does. He looks at the man at the table and says two words: follow me. The gospel records no speech, no debate, no night to think it over.
It records a man standing up. Today, Matthew.

teach.h: ONE VERSE: FOLLOW ME, AND HE AROSE.
teach.b: The whole call takes one verse. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sees a man sitting in the custom house, named Matthew, and says to him: "Follow me. And he arose up and followed him."
Mark and Luke tell the same scene and call the man Levi; Catholic tradition reads Levi and Matthew as one person. Now look at what he left.

teach.h: SOME SAY: NO BOAT TO GO BACK TO.
teach.b: Some readers point to a difference: a fisherman like Peter could go back to his boats, and in John's gospel he does. A man who walked away from a tax post, those readers say, had no boat to go back to.
And what does he do first? Luke says he made Jesus a great feast in his own house. Matthew's gospel says many publicans and sinners came and sat down with Jesus.
Some onlookers asked his disciples why their teacher ate with such people. Jesus answered with a doctor's logic: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill."
Then he sent them to a line from the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy and not sacrifice."

teach.h: HIS FIRST ACT: A DINNER FOR HIS CROWD.
teach.b: So the first thing a newly called man did was invite his old crowd to meet the one who called him. The book that opens the New Testament carries his name, and Catholic tradition holds him to be its author.

teach.h: HE KEPT THE NAME: MATTHEW THE PUBLICAN.
teach.b: In that gospel, the man is named plainly: Matthew the publican.

teach.h: I WILL HAVE MERCY AND NOT SACRIFICE.
teach.b: He kept the old label right next to the new life.

how: The feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, is kept on 21 September with its own Mass readings, often including the call at the tax booth from Matthew 9.

games.q: you're Matthew. you've just walked away from your tax table to follow Jesus. what do you do first?
o: leave town quietly so no one sees
throw a dinner for your old crowd
go back and close the books properly
games.why: Luke says Levi made a great feast in his house, and Matthew's gospel puts publicans and sinners at that table: the new follower brought his old friends along.

practice: Notice what's on your table right now, the thing you keep checking, the stack you keep counting: your phone, a worry, a grudge. For these two minutes, set one down, literally if you can.
If you pray, hear the two words, follow me, and stay with them; if you don't, notice what it feels like to stand up from something.

wordCard.voice: Matthew. The tax collector who heard two words, got up from his table, and then threw a dinner so his old friends could meet the man who called him.

orig.note: the Greek gospel word for a tax collector, the old trade the Douay-Rheims renders as publican.
